headline: Jimmy Carter’s death, violence in the US and a plane crash in South Korea – a look at the world this week
description: From a series of violent incidents in the US and Putin’s ‘apology’ after the Azerbaijan airline crash to heightened tensions between Taiwan and China, the world rang in the new year on a grim note this week.
content:
Welcome to this week’s roundup of key global events and developments shaping politics, economics, and society. From groundbreaking policy shifts and diplomatic manoeuvres to emerging stories of resilience and upheaval, we bring you the latest updates and insights. For Indian audiences, understanding these developments is not just about keeping informed—it’s about identifying the ripple effects that could influence India’s foreign policy and its position in an increasingly fragmented world.
Whether it’s a headline grabbing the world’s attention or an underreported issue with far-reaching consequences, we aim to provide a clear, concise, and comprehensive overview of what matters most.
Jimmy Carter: The best president America ever had?
Jimmy Carter, who passed away at the age of 100, leaves behind a legacy that cements his status as arguably the greatest former president in American history. His post-presidential years were marked by an extraordinary commitment to humanitarian causes, global mediation, and a moral clarity that resonated far beyond political circles. However, his single term in office from 1977 to 1981 remains a contentious chapter, often overshadowed by subsequent challenges.
Presidency of Carter
During his presidency, Carter accomplished a great deal on the global stage. Among his most notable achievements were the Panama Canal Treaties, which transferred control of the canal to Panama; the groundbreaking Camp David Accords, which laid the groundwork for peace between Egypt and Israel; and the SALT II agreement, a key arms control treaty with the Soviet Union. Carter’s tenure also saw NATO adopt a twin-track approach toward the Soviet Union and a pronounced emphasis on human rights in US foreign policy.
Yet these successes were eclipsed by domestic economic troubles, including spiralling inflation, and the Iran hostage crisis, which deeply undermined his administration. The culmination of these issues led to his decisive defeat in the 1980 presidential election to Ronald Reagan.
Post-presidency
Carter’s loss, however, marked the beginning of an inspiring second act. Turning away from the political spotlight, he quietly set about addressing issues that he believed could be solved through dedication, compassion, and expertise. Among his most enduring contributions was his involvement with Habitat for Humanity, a non-profit organisation focused on building affordable housing for those in need. Carter didn’t just lend his name, he personally worked on construction sites, hammer in hand, well into his later years.
Central to his post-presidential work was The Carter Center, established in 1982 at Emory University in Georgia. The centre blended the roles of an international think tank and a conflict-resolution organisation, becoming a hub for efforts to advance peace, health, and democracy worldwide. It was this body of work that earned Carter the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Throughout the 1990s, Carter led international election-monitoring missions across the globe, ensuring fair democratic practices in countries as diverse as Zambia and the Dominican Republic. Earlier, he had played a crucial role in brokering the peace settlement in Ethiopia, which ultimately led to Eritrea’s independence. These efforts epitomised his unwavering belief in diplomacy and grassroots action as tools for change.
A life of service
Carter’s life offers a blueprint for moral leadership. While his presidency may have been marred by challenges, his post-presidential years showcased the profound impact one individual could have in shaping a better world. His ability to rise above political defeat and dedicate himself to service remains an enduring testament to his character. Carter once said, “We must adjust to changing times and still hold to unchanging principles.” His legacy is proof that he lived by those words.
As public affection for Carter lingered, he remained a symbol of hope and resilience, proving that a presidency need not define the full measure of a man’s contributions.
Violence in America: A grim start to the New Year
The United States has been rocked by a series of violent incidents, from terror attacks to tragic accidents, as Americans marked the beginning of the new year. Here is an expanded overview of the most significant events:
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
New Orleans: a city under siege
In a devastating attack on January 1, a man drove a pick-up truck into a crowded Bourbon Street in New Orleans, leaving 10 people dead and 35 injured. The FBI is investigating the incident as an act of terrorism.
Anne Kirkpatrick, superintendent of the New Orleans Police Department, described the horrific scene, stating, “It was very intentional behaviour. This man was trying to run over as many people as he possibly could. He was hell-bent on creating the carnage and the damage that he did.” The suspect, 42-year-old Shamsud-Din Jabbar from Texas, was shot dead in a firefight. He was a US citizen and a former Army Reserve staff sergeant with no apparent history of violence. However, an ISIS flag was found in his rented Ford pick-up truck, along with weapons and potential improvised explosive devices.
The FBI confirmed that they are the lead investigative agency, with officials working tirelessly to uncover Jabbar’s affiliations with terrorist organisations. Bomb technicians are examining the devices found at the scene.
Jabbar, who served in the military for years, was stationed at Fort Bragg at one point and deployed to Afghanistan. His record shows minor infractions from two decades ago, but nothing to suggest the potential for violence.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
New Orleans Mayor LaToya Cantrell called for prayers for the victims, describing the attack as a “terrorist attack.” Meanwhile, President Joe Biden assured the public that every resource is being mobilized to investigate and secure the city. President-elect Donald Trump labelled the incident “an act of pure evil” and pledged full support for the city’s recovery efforts.
The attack occurred amidst heightened activity in New Orleans due to the Sugar Bowl football game. Despite previous warnings in a 2019 security report that Bourbon Street’s bollards were inadequate to prevent vehicular attacks, the barriers remained compromised. The report, commissioned by a New York security firm, highlighted the vulnerability of the French Quarter, citing vehicular ramming and active shooting as the most likely threats. Local officials had started work to replace these barriers in November, but the project was incomplete at the time of the attack.
New Orleans first installed its metal security barriers in 2017, inspired by the devastating Bastille Day truck attack in Nice, France. However, Mardi Gras beads and wear over time rendered these bollards ineffective. Security experts acknowledge that while such measures help, no city can fully guard against determined attackers.
Queens, New York: nightclub shooting leaves 11 injured
In Queens, New York, a shooting outside the Amazura nightclub on January 1 injured 11 people. According to the NYPD, several individuals approached the venue and opened fire over 30 times, striking multiple vehicles and hitting six females and four males, ranging in age from 16 to 20.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
The incident unfolded around 11.18 pm when officers received multiple 911 calls reporting the gunfire. Investigators believe the attackers targeted a group standing in line outside the event. NYPD officials reassured the public that the shooting was not terror-related, though the motives behind the attack remain under investigation.
The nightclub shooting is part of a worrying trend of gun violence that continues to plague communities across the United States. Local residents expressed shock and fear, questioning the adequacy of public safety measures in busy urban areas.
Honolulu: fireworks tragedy
Honolulu witnessed a horrific fireworks explosion on January 1 that killed three people and injured over 20 others. The incident occurred when a large New Year’s firework tipped over, causing a fiery blast that inflicted severe burns and shrapnel wounds.
Hawaii Governor Josh Green lamented the gruesome scene, describing the injuries as “war-zone injuries.” Mayor Rick Blangiardi called the incident “a tragic way to start the new year” and vowed to enforce tougher penalties for illegal fireworks. “We’re angry, frustrated, and deeply saddened at this unnecessary loss of life and suffering,” he said.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Emergency crews faced chaos as they arrived to treat victims, including children. Two women died at the scene, while a third succumbed to her injuries in a hospital. Social media posts revealed that fireworks were being set off across wide areas of Honolulu despite their illegality. Some individuals continued setting off fireworks even as victims were being transported to hospitals.
In a separate incident on Oahu, another fireworks explosion claimed a fourth life, underscoring the pervasiveness of the issue. Governor Green is considering new penalties, including felony charges, to address the persistent problem of illegal fireworks in Hawaii.
Las Vegas: explosive incident outside Trump Hotel
In Las Vegas, a Tesla Cybertruck filled with fuel canisters and fireworks exploded outside the Trump Hotel, killing the driver and injuring seven others. Dramatic footage showed the vehicle parked near the hotel entrance before erupting in a devastating blast.
Authorities identified the driver as Matthew Alan Livelsberger, an active-duty US Army service member. Livelsberger had been awarded multiple commendations for valour during his five combat deployments in Afghanistan. Investigators confirmed that he died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound moments before the explosion.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Sheriff Kevin McMahill displayed footage of the incident and photographs of the truck’s contents, which included several fuel canisters and large fireworks. McMahill noted the vehicle was rented in Colorado and arrived in Las Vegas just hours before the detonation.
The FBI is exploring potential connections between this incident and the New Orleans attack. “Obviously, a Cybertruck, the Trump Hotel, there’s lots of questions that we have to answer as we move forward,” McMahill said. While no evidence has linked Livelsberger to ISIS, authorities remain cautious, noting the unusual circumstances of the case.
Azerbaijan airline crash and Putin’s ‘apology’
The tragic downing of an Azerbaijan Airlines plane this past week has left 38 people dead and raised international tensions. President Vladimir V Putin of Russia broke a three-day silence to offer an apology to Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev but stopped short of explicitly acknowledging Russian responsibility.
In a phone call initiated by Putin, the Kremlin confirmed that the crash occurred in Russian airspace as Russian air defences were repelling a Ukrainian drone attack near Grozny Airport. Aviation experts and US officials, however, believe a Russian air-defence missile mistakenly struck the Embraer 190 airliner travelling from Baku, Azerbaijan, to Grozny. The plane was diverted from its path and eventually crashed in Aktau, Kazakhstan, after crossing the Caspian Sea.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Of the 67 people onboard, 29 survived, but the fatalities included seven Russians, six Kazakhs, and 25 Azerbaijani citizens. Survivors described a loud banging noise and fragments entering the cabin, which injured a flight attendant. Initial Russian reports blamed fog and birds but subsequent investigations have focused on a potential missile strike.
Relationship between Azerbaijan and Russia
The crash has complicated relations between Azerbaijan and Russia. The two nations share a history fraught with suspicion, dating back to Azerbaijan’s brief independence after World War I and its eventual incorporation into the Soviet Union. Since gaining independence in 1991, Azerbaijan has balanced its ties with Moscow amid ongoing conflicts over Nagorno-Karabakh, where Russia has acted as both a mediator and an arms supplier.
The Kremlin’s partial acceptance of responsibility has drawn comparisons to a 2020 incident when Azerbaijan swiftly apologised for accidentally downing a Russian military helicopter. In an interview with Al Jazeera, Farhad Mammadov, director of the Baku-based Center for Studies of the South Caucasus, noted the disparity in responses: “Azerbaijan is expecting the same now, which we have not seen yet. If the Russian side has chosen the path of partial apology, we will expect subsequent apologies, punishments, and compensations.”
US President Joe Biden, speaking from the Virgin Islands, cautiously acknowledged Putin’s statement, saying, “Apparently he did, but I haven’t spoken to him.” As investigations continue, the crash has further strained an already tense geopolitical climate, highlighting the perils of conflict spillover into civilian domains.
South Korea’s aviation tragedy
In one of South Korea’s most devastating aviation disasters, a Jeju Air passenger jet crashed and erupted into flames during its landing at Muan International Airport on December 29, 2024, claiming the lives of 179 individuals. The flight, returning from Bangkok, carried 181 people on board, including six crew members. Tragically, only two crew members were rescued from the tail section of the Boeing 737-800 aircraft, while all other passengers and crew perished in the incident, according to South Korea’s national fire agency.
The South Korean Ministry of Transport reported that among the 175 passengers, 173 were South Korean nationals, and two were Thai citizens. The crash now stands as the worst commercial aviation accident since the 2018 Lion Air Flight 610 disaster in Indonesia, which killed 189 people, as noted by the Aviation Safety Network.
Investigation focus: the role of runway infrastructure
Authorities are investigating the circumstances leading to this catastrophic event, with particular attention on the embankment at the runway’s end. The hardened barrier, housing an essential localiser antenna system that guides aircraft during landings, was struck by the Jeju Air flight after its failed landing attempt. While this structure plays a critical role in navigation, questions are being raised about its proximity to the runway — only 199 metres (652 feet) away — far below the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO’s) recommended safety area of 240 metres, though it meets the mandated minimum of 90 metres.
The Chosun Ilbo newspaper revealed that an airport operating manual, updated earlier in 2024, highlighted this issue. At the time, airport officials reportedly stated that “adjustments would be considered” during future developments but no action appears to have been taken.
Unanswered questions
Investigators face numerous unresolved questions, including why the plane landed late on the runway at high speed without deploying its landing gear or using wing flaps to decelerate. Initial theories speculated a bird strike, but experts remain sceptical, suggesting that such an event would not typically prevent the deployment of landing gear.
The jet’s CFM International 56-7B26 engines were reportedly functioning as the pilot attempted a belly landing, raising further concerns about whether any control systems were compromised. Investigators are also scrutinising the decision to land shortly after declaring an emergency, a choice that has left aviation experts perplexed.
Government’s response
The crash presents a significant challenge for South Korea’s acting president, Choi Sang-mok, who recently took office following the impeachment of his predecessor, Han Duck-soo. Choi has initiated an emergency safety inspection of the nation’s airline operations and directed the transport ministry to examine all 101 Boeing 737-800 aircraft currently in service within the country by the end of the week.
In a disaster management meeting, Choi emphasised the government’s commitment to supporting the victims’ families and ensuring transparency in the investigation process. “Even before the final results are out, we ask that officials transparently disclose the accident investigation process and promptly inform the bereaved families,” he stated.
As South Korea mourns this tragic loss, the investigation’s findings will be crucial in determining accountability and preventing future disasters of this magnitude.
Russia-Ukraine: Prisoner swaps and gas transit disruptions
In a significant development just before New Year’s Eve, Russia and Ukraine exchanged over 300 prisoners, marking the 59th swap since the onset of the full-scale invasion. This exchange, partially facilitated by the United Arab Emirates, highlights the ongoing complexities of the war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the exchange via Telegram, stating: “The return of our people from Russian captivity is always very good news. Today, we managed to bring 189 Ukrainians home,” as reported by The Guardian. However, the Russian defense ministry announced that 150 prisoners from each side had been returned, underscoring discrepancies in the reported numbers.
This exchange was one of the largest to date, with the released Ukrainians including soldiers, border guards, National Guardsmen, and Navy servicemen. Many had endured over two and a half years in captivity, and several returned with severe illnesses and injuries. While this brought relief to some families, thousands more Ukrainians remain in captivity, with Kyiv estimating the number of prisoners held by Russia to exceed 8,000.
Negotiating prisoner exchanges has grown increasingly difficult, according to Ukrainian officials. The stalemate coincides with significant advances by Russian forces, compounding the challenges.
Russian gas flows
Amid these humanitarian developments, a major economic shift unfolded as Russian gas flows through Ukraine ceased on January 1 following the expiration of a transit agreement. This pipeline, one of the last two routes delivering Russian gas to Europe, carried profound implications for both the region’s energy dynamics and the ongoing conflict.
The pipeline’s closure removes approximately 5 per cent of the European Union’s gas imports during the peak winter heating season. Slovakia, heavily reliant on this route, is particularly affected. Analysts suggest the halt could lead to heightened European demand for liquefied natural gas (LNG), further intensifying competition with Asia for pricier alternatives.
The now-expired deal was brokered at the end of 2019, just before the previous 10-year agreement between national gas companies lapsed. While the European Commission initially supported the agreement, the 2022 invasion of Ukraine prompted a policy shift, urging member states to diversify energy supplies and reduce dependence on Russian fossil fuels. Despite this, Russia-friendly governments in Hungary and Slovakia sought extensions, reflecting divided EU strategies.
Ukraine pre-emptively signalled its intent to terminate the agreement, aiming to deprive Russia of gas export revenues. According to the Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, the cessation could cost Russia approximately $6.5 billion unless alternative routes are secured. However, the decision also poses financial challenges for Ukraine, which earned $1 billion annually in transit fees, with only a fifth of that representing gross profit. Analysts warn that Ukraine’s extensive gas infrastructure might face increased attacks if it no longer facilitates Russian gas transit.
Gazprom, Russia’s state-owned energy giant, blamed Ukraine for the agreement’s collapse, stating in a Telegram post: “Since 8:00 Moscow time, the supply of Russian gas for its transportation through the territory of Ukraine has not been carried out.”
Despite these tensions, EU officials remain confident in the region’s ability to adapt. The European Commission emphasised: “European gas infrastructure is flexible enough to provide gas of non-Russian origin to central and eastern Europe via alternative routes.” It highlighted significant investments in LNG import capacities since 2022, designed to fortify Europe’s energy security.
This dual narrative of humanitarian progress and economic upheaval underscores the multifaceted impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, where prisoner exchanges and gas diplomacy reveal the intertwining of geopolitical and human stakes.
Heightened tensions between Taiwan and China
Chinese President Xi Jinping marked the New Year with a forceful message, reiterating that no power can obstruct China’s “reunification” with Taiwan. Delivered on Tuesday, his statement was widely interpreted as a warning to both Taiwan’s pro-independence factions and its international allies.
Over the past year, Beijing has escalated its military manoeuvres around Taiwan. These actions include repeated incursions by Chinese warships and aircraft into Taiwan’s surrounding waters and airspace. Taiwanese officials have characterised these incursions as a strategy to “normalise” China’s military presence in the region, raising concerns about Beijing’s long-term intentions.
On Thursday, Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense reported that Chinese warplanes and warships had conducted the year’s first “combat patrol” around the island. This development followed Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te’s renewed call for dialogue with Beijing.
Taiwan’s defense ministry detailed the scope of these operations, revealing that 22 Chinese military aircraft, including J-16 fighter jets, participated in a “joint combat readiness patrol” in coordination with Chinese warships starting Thursday morning.
Taiwanese sovereignty
Taipei’s government, firmly rejecting Beijing’s sovereignty claims, maintains that Taiwan’s future can only be decided by its 23 million residents. In his New Year’s Day address, President Lai reiterated his willingness to engage in talks with China, underscoring Taiwan’s commitment to dialogue. However, Beijing has dismissed such overtures, branding Lai a “separatist.” This is consistent with its broader stance, having conducted two rounds of military drills around Taiwan last year.
Xi Jinping’s rhetoric aligns with his earlier declarations, including a New Year’s speech last year, in which he insisted that Taiwan’s reunification with China is “inevitable.” He called on people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait to “be bound by a common sense of purpose and share in the glory of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.”
This intensifying dynamic underscores the deepening tensions across the Taiwan Strait, with Beijing continuing its assertive policies and Taipei steadfast in its calls for democratic self-determination. The situation remains a focal point of regional and global geopolitical concern.

headline: Judge sets January 10 date for sentencing Trump in hush money case but rules out prison term
description: Trump has consistently denied any wrongdoing, arguing the case is politically motivated and aimed at damaging his 2024 presidential bid.
content:
Donald Trump is set to be sentenced on January 10 for his hush-money case in New York, just before his anticipated inauguration as president. This comes after Trump failed to have his conviction overturned, with the judge signaling that he won’t face prison time.
Justice Juan Merchan has indicated that Trump is unlikely to face jail time, probation, or a fine. Instead, the judge is expected to grant a “conditional discharge,” meaning Trump could avoid serious penalties. Trump may attend the sentencing either in person or virtually, as reported by BBC. 
Also read | New York judge pauses proceedings in Trump hush money case
The case stems from a $130,000 (£105,000) payment made by Trump’s former lawyer, Michael Cohen, to adult-film star Stormy Daniels during the 2016 election campaign to prevent her from speaking out about an alleged affair with Trump. Trump was convicted in May of 34 felony counts for falsifying business records connected to the payment.
Trump has consistently denied any wrongdoing, arguing the case is politically motivated and aimed at damaging his 2024 presidential bid. His spokesperson, Steven Cheung, condemned the legal proceedings as a “witch hunt” and insisted that Trump should not be sentenced while he is preparing for office.

However, Justice Merchan ruled that the conviction was valid and that the case would move forward, although Trump may still attempt to appeal the verdict after sentencing.
Trump, 78, is currently set to become the first convicted felon to serve as president. He faces additional legal battles, including charges involving classified documents and efforts to overturn the 2020 election results.

headline: Israeli airstrikes kill at least 54 across Gaza, medics say
description: The Israeli military said it had conducted an intelligence-based strike in Al-Mawasi, just west of the city of Khan Younis, and eliminated Shahwan, calling him the head of Hamas security forces in southern Gaza. It made no mention of Salah's death.
content:
Israeli airstrikes killed at least Palestinians across the Gaza Strip on Thursday, including 11 people in a tent encampment sheltering displaced families, medics said. They said the 11 included women and children in the Al-Mawasi district, which was designated as a humanitarian zone for civilians earlier in the war between Israel and Gaza’s ruling Hamas militant group, now in its 15th month.
The director general of Gaza’s police department, Mahmoud Salah, and his aide, Hussam Shahwan, were killed in the strike, according to the Hamas-run Gaza interior ministry.
“By committing the crime of assassinating the director general of police in the Gaza Strip, the occupation is insisting on spreading chaos in the (enclave) and deepening the human suffering of citizens,” it added in a statement.
The Israeli military said it had conducted an intelligence-based strike in Al-Mawasi, just west of the city of Khan Younis, and eliminated Shahwan, calling him the head of Hamas security forces in southern Gaza. It made no mention of Salah’s death.
STORIES YOU MAY LIKE

Watch | Before spat with Trump, Zelenskyy was asked why he is not wearing a suit. His reply
Trump is building a new American empire
Other Israeli airstrikes killed at least 43 Palestinians, including six in the interior ministry headquarters in Khan Younis and others in north Gaza’s Jabalia refugee camp, the Shati (Beach) camp and central Gaza’s Maghazi camp.
Israel’s military said it had targeted Hamas militants who intelligence indicated were operating in a command and control centre “embedded inside the Khan Younis municipality building in the Humanitarian Area”.
“As the year begins, we got reports of yet another attack on Al-Mawasi with dozens of people killed, another reminder that there is no humanitarian zone let alone a safe zone (in Gaza)”, Philippe Lazzarini, head of the U.N. agency for Palestinian refugees UNRWA, said in a post on X.
“Everyday without a ceasefire will bring more tragedy.”

Asked about Thursday’s reported death toll, a spokesperson for the Israeli military said it followed international law in waging the war in Gaza and that it took “feasible precautions to mitigate civilian harm”.
Later on Thursday, separate Israeli airstrikes killed at least four people on Jala Street in downtown Gaza City and two in its Zeitoun district, medics said.
The Israeli military has accused Gaza militants of using built-up residential areas for cover. Hamas denies this.
Hamas’ smaller ally Islamic Jihad said it fired rockets into the southern Israeli kibbutz of Holit near Gaza on Thursday. The Israeli military said it intercepted one projectile in the area that had crossed from southern Gaza.

Israel has killed more than 45,500 Palestinians in the war, according to Gaza’s health ministry. Most of Gaza’s 2.3 million people have been displaced and much of the tiny, heavily built-up coastal territory is in ruins.
The war was triggered by Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023 cross-border attack on southern Israel in which 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage to Gaza, according to Israeli tallies

headline: Watch: Moment when Tesla Cybertruck burst into flames outside Trump’s Las Vegas hotel
description: Tesla CEO Elon Musk addressed the incident on X, confirming that vehicles involved in both incidents were rented from the same car rental site, Turo.
content:
A Tesla Cybertruck burst into flames outside the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas on Wednesday morning, leaving the driver dead and seven others injured. Authorities, including the FBI, are investigating whether the incident was an act of terrorism, officials informed.
Las Vegas Sheriff Kevin McMahill, while providing details about the explosion, also shared a video of the blast. The explosion occurred around 8:40 am when the 2024 Tesla Cybertruck arrived at the hotel’s valet area. “Shortly after the vehicle pulled in, smoke was observed coming from inside the truck, followed by a flash and a violent explosion,” McMahill explained.
Police release video showing Cybertruck explode outside Las Vegas Trump Hotel. (Screengrab)
The video revealed the severity of the blast. While the sole occupant of the Cybertruck, the driver, was killed, seven bystanders sustained minor injuries. Two of the injured were transported to nearby hospitals. The Trump International Hotel was evacuated, and guests were relocated to another property.
The investigation has drawn comparisons to another attack earlier that day in New Orleans, where a rented Ford F-150 was found with a suspected explosive device. Notably, both vehicles were rented through the car-sharing platform Turo.
Appears likely to be an act of terrorism.
Both this Cybertruck and the F-150 suicide bomb in New Orleans were rented from Turo. Perhaps they are linked in some way. https://t.co/MM6ehJO3SG
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) January 1, 2025
Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who has publicly supported Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, addressed the incident on X, confirming that vehicles involved in both incidents were rented from the same car rental site, Turo.
“Appears likely to be an act of terrorism. Both this Cybertruck and the F-150 suicide bomb in New Orleans were rented from Turo. Perhaps they are linked in some way,” he wrote.
Musk also noted, “We have now confirmed that the explosion was caused by very large fireworks and/or a bomb carried in the bed of the rented Cybertruck and is unrelated to the vehicle itself.”
“All vehicle telemetry was positive at the time of the explosion,” he said.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
The Trump International Hotel, part of the Trump Organization, was evacuated as a precaution. Firefighters arrived within four minutes of the blast and quickly extinguished the flames.

headline: Federal court upholds $5 million verdict in sexual abuse case against Trump
description: The $5m included $2.02m for sexual assault and $2.98m for defamation related to Trump’s 2022 social media post
content:
A federal appeals court has upheld a $5 million verdict against Donald Trump for sexually abusing and defaming magazine writer E Jean Carroll, marking a legal setback for the president-elect, The Guardian reported.
The three-judge panel at the second US circuit court of appeals in Manhattan rejected Trump’s appeal for a new trial. They ruled that evidence, including testimonies from other women who accused Trump of sexual misconduct and the infamous Access Hollywood tape, was properly admitted in court. The tape famously recorded Trump boasting about grabbing women.
The verdict, handed down in May 2023, found Trump liable for sexually assaulting Carroll in a New York department store dressing room in the mid-1990s, before he became president. However, the jury did not label the incident as rape. The $5m included $2.02m for sexual assault and $2.98m for defamation related to Trump’s 2022 social media post, where he dismissed Carroll’s accusations as a “hoax”.
Also read | Donald Trump weighs in on H-1B: Been a believer… great programme
The appeals court found that testimonies from two other women, businesswoman Jessica Leeds and former People magazine writer Natasha Stoynoff, were crucial in establishing a pattern of behaviour consistent with Carroll’s allegations. “Mr. Trump’s statements in the Access Hollywood tape, together with the testimony of Ms Leeds and Ms Stoynoff, establish a repeated, idiosyncratic pattern of conduct consistent with what Ms Carroll alleged,” the court said, according to The Guardian.

Donald Trump orders investigation on US lumber imports ahead of likely tariffs
Carroll’s attorney, Roberta Kaplan, said in a statement, “Both E Jean Carroll and I are gratified by today’s decision. We thank the second circuit for its careful consideration of the parties’ arguments,” as reported by The Guardian.
Also read | Trump says extension of the debt ceiling will ‘go down as one of the dumbest political decisions made in years’
The ruling follows a separate defamation verdict in January 2024, when Carroll won $83.3m after Trump denied her allegations in 2019. Trump is appealing that verdict as well. Trump has consistently denied all the accusations, claiming he never met Carroll and that she was “not his type”.
Despite the ruling, the case is expected to continue after Trump’s second presidential term begins on 20 January 2025. The US Supreme Court ruled in 1997 that sitting presidents do not have immunity from civil litigation over actions that occurred before they took office.

headline: Biden pays tribute to Manmohan Singh, credits him for strengthening US-India ties
description: He praised Singh for his role in key initiatives, including the US-India Civil Nuclear Agreement and the formation of the first Quad partnership among Indo-Pacific nations.
content:
US President Joe Biden has expressed deep sorrow over the passing of former Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, hailing him as “a true statesman” who played a key role in enhancing the US-India partnership. Singh, who served as India’s Prime Minister from 2004 to 2014, passed away in New Delhi on Thursday at the age of 92.
Biden, in a statement, credited Singh’s leadership and vision for fostering historic levels of cooperation between the two nations. “The unprecedented level of cooperation between the United States and India today would not have been possible without Prime Minister Singh’s strategic vision and political courage,” Biden said, as reported by PTI.
Also read | As Biden makes way for Trump, Jaishankar goes to US for talks on deepening relations
He praised Singh for his role in key initiatives, including the US-India Civil Nuclear Agreement and the formation of the first Quad partnership among Indo-Pacific nations. “These achievements charted progress that will continue to strengthen our nations—and the world—for generations to come. He was a true statesman, a dedicated public servant, and above all, a kind and humble person,” Biden added.
Reflecting on his personal interactions with Singh, Biden recounted meeting him in various capacities, including as Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in 2008, as Vice President during Singh’s State Visit to the US in 2009, and during Biden’s visit to New Delhi in 2013. “As we discussed then, the US-India relationship is among the most consequential in the world,” Biden said, PTI reported.
Also read | Biden signs defence bill despite objections to ban on transgender healthcare for children
He emphasised Singh’s enduring impact, saying, “During this difficult time, we recommit to the vision to which Prime Minister Singh dedicated his life. Together, as partners and friends, our nations can unlock a future of dignity and unlimited potential for all of our people.”
Biden extended his condolences to Singh’s wife, Gursharan Kaur, their children, and the people of India. “Jill and I send our deepest condolences,” he concluded.

headline: Gaza medics say Israeli strike kills five journalists, Israel says it hit militants
description: The Palestinian Journalists Union said one strike killed five journalists from the Al-Quds Today channel who were in a broadcast vehicle in front of Al-Awda Hospital in the Al-Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza.
content:
Gaza authorities said an Israeli airstrike killed five Palestinian journalists in a vehicle outside a hospital on Thursday but the Israeli army said the victims were Islamic Jihad militants posing as media workers.
Medics said the five were among at least 31 people killed in Israeli air assaults across the Palestinian enclave before dawn as Hamas and Israel traded blame over delays in reaching a ceasefire deal after more than 14 months of fighting.
The Palestinian Journalists Union said one strike killed five journalists from the Al-Quds Today channel who were in a broadcast vehicle in front of Al-Awda Hospital in the Al-Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza.
The union said more than 190 Palestinian journalists have been killed by Israeli fire since the war began in October 2023.
The Gaza-based channel called the strike a massacre and said in a statement on Telegram the five “were killed as they carried out their media and humanitarian duty”. It has regularly featured Islamic Jihad leaders and provided day-to-day coverage of the war in Gaza.
The Israeli military said it “conducted a precise strike on a vehicle with an Islamic Jihad terrorist cell inside in the area of Nuseirat”.
Later, it issued a statement listing the names of the five TV crewmen and saying: “Intelligence from multiple sources confirmed that these individuals were Islamic Jihad operatives posing as journalists.”
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Israel has regularly denied targeting journalists and says it takes steps to avoid hitting civilians.
The Iranian-backed Islamic Jihad group, an ally of Hamas, fought several rounds against Israel in the past two decades, and fighters of the group have joined the fighting against Israel since October 2023. It said it has hostages in its custody too.
The group condemned Israel’s killing of the five men in a statement but it did not claim any of them as a member.
Later on Thursday, health officials said five medical staff, including a pediatrician, were killed by Israeli fire at Kamal Adwan Hospital in Beit Lahiya in the northern edge of Gaza Strip, where Israeli forces have operated since October.
There was no Israeli comment on the medics’ death.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
The officials there said they had resisted army orders to evacuate the hospital since the new ground offensive began nearly three months ago.
The Israeli military, which on Wednesday said the hospital was in the heart of the complex fighting, renewed the evacuation orders three days ago, Gaza medics said.
Israel’s campaign against Hamas in Gaza has killed more than 45,300 Palestinians, according to health officials in the Hamas-run enclave. Most of the population of 2.3 million has been displaced and much of Gaza is in ruins.
The war was triggered by Hamas’ attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, in which 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage to Gaza, according to Israeli tallies.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
FUNERALS
Video from the scene of Thursday’s attack showed the twisted wreckage of a white van with what appeared to be the remnants of the word “PRESS” in red on the back doors.
Later on Thursday, dozens of relatives and fellow journalists took part in the funerals of the five journalists, whose bodies were wrapped in white shrouds. Blue flak jackets bearing the word “PRESS” were placed on top of the shrouded bodies.
“The Israeli army justifies or excuses this targeting by claiming it is aimed at individuals involved in Palestinian organizations and cells. However, on the ground, these individuals were on journalistic assignments, residing in press vehicles and covering events,” said Abed Meqdad, a correspondent for Al-Araby TV channel during the funerals.
Women wept besides the bodies as men performed special prayers before burials.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“May God take revenge on them, may God take revenge on them. He’s the one that makes the news and broadcasts the crimes to the world, this is what they do to them,” said the mother of Fadi Hassouna, one of the dead journalists.
In its end-of-year report, the Reporters Without Borders organisation said Gaza was the world’s most dangerous region for journalists due to killings by the Israeli army.
Medics in the enclave said 13 other people were killed and 25 wounded in an Israeli airstrike on a house in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood. The death toll could rise as many people were trapped under the rubble, they added.
In Gaza City, an Israeli strike on a house in the suburb of Sabra killed eight more people, medics said, bringing Thursday’s death toll to 31.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
On Wednesday, Hamas and Israel traded blame over their failure to conclude a ceasefire agreement despite progress reported by both sides in past days.
Hamas said Israel had laid down further conditions, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the group of going back on understandings already reached.
“The occupation has set new conditions related to withdrawal, ceasefire, prisoners, and the return of the displaced, which has delayed reaching the agreement that was available,” Hamas said.
Netanyahu responded in a statement: “The Hamas terrorist organization continues to lie, is reneging on understandings that have already been reached, and is continuing to create difficulties in the negotiations.”

headline: At least 2 journalists killed, several wounded in gang attack during Haiti hospital reopening
description: The attack by the gang members on Christmas Eve also led to the casualty of a police officer, however, the status of the officer is not known till now, AP reported.
content:
In a gang attack in Haiti on Tuesday, two journalists were killed and several others were injured during the reopening of Port-au-Prince’s biggest public hospital, Associated Press reported.
The General Hospital in Haiti’s capital was forcibly closed earlier this year by street gangs but the administration had vowed to reopen the facility in Port-au-Prince. But suspected gang members opened fire as journalists gathered to cover the reopening of the hospital.
The attack by the gang members on Christmas Eve also led to the casualty of a police officer, however, the status of the officer is not known till now, AP reported.
The deceased journalists were identified as Markenzy Nathoux and Jimmy Jean. A spokesperson of the Online Media Collective, Robest Dimanche, said an unspecified number of reporters were also been in the attack.
The wife of a journalist, who was shot during an armed gang attack on the General Hospital, cries as an ambulance arrives with his body, at a different hospital in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Tuesday. (AP Photo)
Haiti’s interim president, Leslie Voltaire, condemned the attack and said that journalists and police were among the victims but did not specify the number of casualties in the incident.
“I send my sympathies to the people who were victims, the national police and the journalists,” Voltaire said.
His government in a statement said that they are “responding firmly to the attack”. “This heinous act, which targets an institution dedicated to health and life, constitutes an unacceptable attack on the very foundations of our society,” the government added.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
According to AP, the Radio Télé Métronome posted earlier that seven journalists and two police officers were wounded in the suspected gang attack during the hospital reopening.
In a purported video posted online, Johnson “Izo” André, who is considered to be one of the most powerful gang leaders in Haiti, claimed responsibility for the attack. The video allegedly claimed that the gang of coalition had not authorized the hospital reopening.

headline: Turkish Foreign Minister says no room for Kurdish militants in Syria’s future
description: The minister stated that discussions with the Syrian administration focused on ensuring Syria’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.
content:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan declared there is no place for Kurdish militants in Syria’s future, reported Reuters, emphasizing the need for the YPG militia to disband. Fidan made the remarks during a visit to Damascus, the first by a Turkish foreign minister since the fall of Bashar al-Assad two weeks ago.
Fidan met with Syria’s de facto leader Ahmed al-Sharaa amid ongoing hostilities between Turkish-backed Syrian forces and the US-aligned Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which the YPG spearheads. Turkey views the YPG as an extension of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), a group designated as a terrorist organization by Ankara, Washington, and the European Union.
Fidan stated that discussions with the Syrian administration focused on ensuring Syria’s territorial integrity and sovereignty. “In the coming period, the YPG must come to a point where it is no longer a threat to Syria’s national unity,” he said, urging the militia to disband.
Also Read: | Turkey will do ‘whatever it takes’ if Syria govt can’t address Kurd militia issue, minister says
The SDF played a crucial role in defeating Islamic State militants from 2014 to 2017 with US support. However, the group now faces growing threats from Ankara and its allies, as well as shifting dynamics under Syria’s new leadership, which maintains close ties with Turkey.
Fidan also criticized the international community for overlooking the SDF and YPG’s “illegal” actions but expressed optimism that US President-elect Donald Trump would take a different approach. Syria’s administration has indicated a willingness to manage Islamic State prison camps if needed, according to Fidan.
Also Read: | 2 Kurdish journalists killed in Syria, allegedly in Turkish drone
Turkey has conducted multiple cross-border offensives against Kurdish factions in northern Syria and controls territory along the border. Ankara continues to demand that the US halt support for the Kurdish fighters.
Meanwhile, Syria’s new leadership, including the Turkish-backed Syrian National Army, is expected to move against YPG-held territories.

headline: At least 38 people killed as bus and truck collide in Brazil
description: The exact number remains uncertain due to the severely burned condition of the victims' bodies, requiring forensic identification.
content:
More than 30 people have been killed in a “tragic” traffic collision between a bus and truck  on Saturday in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais, the Reuters reported, citing fire department officials who attended the scene.
The incident occurred near Teófilo Otoni in Minas Gerais on the BR-116 highway. After removing all of the victims,  authorities reported the death toll to be 38, including the bus driver.
Firefighters said they rescued 13 passengers from the wrecked bus, who were hospitalised in a local hospital.
Meanwhile, the truck driver fled the scene, authorities said.
Initial reports suggested a tire blowout caused the bus, en route from São Paulo to Bahia, carrying 45 passengers, to lose control and collide with the truck.
A person inspects the scene of a traffic accident after a packed bus collided with a truck, at the Fernao Dias national highway, near Teofilo Otoni, Brazil, December 21, 2024. Belo Horizonte Military Fire Department/­Handout via REUTERS
However, as per the witnesses cited by Reuters, a granite block from the truck might have fallen onto the road, leading to the collision.
“Only the forensic investigation will confirm the true version,” said the fire department in a statement.
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva expressed his condolences on social media. “I deeply mourn and extend my prayers to the families of the more than 30 victims of the accident in Teofilo Otoni, Minas Gerais. I pray for the recovery of the survivors of this terrible tragedy,” Lula wrote on X.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Another car then collided with the bus, but all three of its passengers survived, according to the fire department. The crash, which took place around 4 am, caused the bus to burst into flames, Reuters reported.
Minas Gerais Governor Romeu Zema expressed condolences on X, announcing full mobilisation of security forces and the deployment of aircraft to assist in rescue operations. “We are working to ensure the families of the victims are supported in this tragic incident, especially during this significant time of the year,” he said.

headline: A Russian general assassinated, Trump’s Nato push, and the US military campaign in Syria – a look at world events this week
description: From Russian Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov’s killing to new revelations highlighting Bashar al-Assad’s reliance on Moscow, a lot has happened in the world this week.
content:
Welcome to this week’s roundup of key global events and developments shaping politics, economics, and society. From groundbreaking policy shifts and diplomatic manoeuvres to emerging stories of resilience and upheaval, we bring you the latest updates and insights. For Indian audiences, understanding these developments is not just about keeping informed — it’s about identifying the ripple effects that could influence India’s foreign policy and its position in an increasingly fragmented world.
Whether it’s a headline grabbing the world’s attention or an underreported issue with far-reaching consequences, we aim to provide a clear, concise, and comprehensive overview of what matters most.
Nato spending
US President-elect Donald Trump is shaking up Nato’s defence spending landscape. Reports indicate Trump’s team has told European officials that he intends to demand member states raise their defence budgets to 5 per cent of GDP — more than double the current 2 per cent target, which only 23 of Nato’s 32 members currently meet.
This dramatic increase comes as Nato allies are already debating a rise to 3 per cent during their upcoming leadership meeting in June. Key members like France, Germany, and the UK are wary of the fiscal strain this could impose. The proposed hike would likely necessitate significant policy adjustments, particularly for countries already grappling with tight budgets.
Trump’s approach to NATO has long been controversial.
During his initial White House campaign, he threatened to withdraw US support for allies unless they contributed more to defence. He also proposed cutting off aid to Ukraine and pushing Kyiv into immediate peace talks. However, sources now suggest that while Trump remains opposed to Ukrainian Nati membership, he plans to continue US military aid to Ukraine, believing it aligns with his vision of achieving “peace through strength.”
This shift provides cautious optimism for European allies. German Chancellor Olaf Scholz, after a recent call with Trump, expressed confidence that “the US and Europe will continue their support to Ukraine.” Meanwhile, British officials have visited Washington to gauge Trump’s potential policy directions, underlining the high stakes for Nato’s future cohesion.
For Nato, the stakes go beyond budgets. Trump’s insistence on burden-sharing reflects his broader scepticism of multilateral commitments, but his readiness to maintain arms supplies to Ukraine hints at a pragmatic streak. As European capitals brace for these demands, the question remains: how much unity can Nato muster under such pressure?
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Cash sent by Assad to Moscow
New revelations highlight Syrian President Bashar al-Assad’s reliance on Moscow during his nation’s darkest days. Between 2018 and 2019, Assad’s central bank reportedly airlifted over $250 million in cash directly to Moscow’s Vnukovo airport. These funds were deposited in sanctioned Russian banks, underscoring the deepening financial and military ties between Syria and Russia.
The Financial Times uncovered these transactions, showing that while Syria’s economy struggled under the weight of war, Assad’s regime prioritised payments to its primary military ally.
The cash transfers coincided with significant Russian involvement in Syria’s war effort. Russian military advisers bolstered Assad’s forces, while Moscow-based companies integrated into Syria’s critical phosphate supply chains. Despite Assad’s dependency on Kremlin support, critics, including former regime loyalists, view these actions as prioritising personal survival over national sovereignty.
The financial arrangements go deeper. Assad’s relatives and close associates reportedly moved substantial assets into Russia during this period. First Lady Asma al-Assad, with her background as a JP Morgan banker, played a pivotal role in consolidating regime control over Syria’s shattered economy. Meanwhile, Assad’s allies were linked to illicit networks, including drug trafficking and fuel smuggling, as noted by US sanctions authorities.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
In addition to direct cash shipments, Assad’s regime benefited from Iranian-backed schemes funnelling hard currency into Syria. Figures like Yassar Ibrahim, Assad’s economic adviser, leveraged companies tied to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps to move millions of dollars for the regime’s benefit.
These financial manoeuvres demonstrate Assad’s strategy to survive and consolidate power, even as his government faces widespread accusations of looting national wealth and engaging in criminal enterprises. For Russia, the partnership ensures a foothold in Syria and strengthens economic and military ties, further complicating the regional and global power dynamic.
US ramps up military campaign in Syria
The United States has significantly intensified its military campaign in Syria, aiming to prevent the resurgence of ISIS amid the chaos left by the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime. In a sharp escalation, US forces have conducted over 75 airstrikes in the past two weeks, targeting ISIS leaders and training camps. These strikes have resulted in the deaths of at least 12 militants and have hit areas previously under the control of Syrian regime forces and Russia, one of Assad’s key international allies.
This surge in military activity coincides with the regime’s collapse, following Assad’s December 8 flight to Moscow as rebel forces captured Damascus. The rapid developments underscore US concerns about the risks posed by ISIS’s ability to exploit the current instability.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
General Michael Kurilla, head of the US Central Command (CENTCOM), visited northeastern Syria during this critical period. His visit included discussions with American troops and the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), Washington’s primary partner in the fight against ISIS. The SDF, a Kurdish-led coalition, has played a pivotal role in combating ISIS but faces increasing threats from regional actors, complicating the United States’ efforts to stabilise the region.
National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan articulated the administration’s worries, emphasising the stakes of the current moment. “The single biggest risk I see is that ISIS comes back because ISIS wants to take advantage of any vacuum or instability in Syria following a civil war. I will not sugar-coat it. This is a real threat — the threat of jihadism and terrorism returning in Syria,” he said.
Syria remains a critical node in ISIS’s global operations. The country was once part of the group’s self-proclaimed “caliphate,” which at its peak stretched across large parts of Iraq and Syria, controlling territory roughly the size of Britain. While international coalitions dealt a decisive blow to ISIS by 2019, dismantling its territorial base, the group has adapted, operating as an underground network with sleeper cells spread across the region.
CENTCOM estimates there are still about 2,500 active ISIS fighters across Iraq and Syria. These militants operate mainly in isolated pockets of central and eastern Syria, often in areas previously controlled by the Assad regime and Russian forces. This year, ISIS has become increasingly active, with CENTCOM reporting 153 attacks in the first half of the year alone — double the activity recorded in the same period in 2023. Analysts, however, believe the situation may be even graver.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Charles Lister, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, noted in a recent report: “The reality is far worse than CENTCOM suggests. ISIS claims only a fraction of its attacks, and we’ve seen an increase in the scale and complexity of their operations, including coordinated ambushes, assassinations, and assaults on oil and gas facilities.”
Adding to the complexity of the situation is the fractured landscape of post-Assad Syria. The fall of the regime has created a power vacuum that multiple actors are vying to fill. Turkey, one of the most influential foreign players in Syria, has declared that its strategic priority is to neutralise Kurdish militants associated with the SDF. Turkey’s military presence in northern Syria and its support for the Syrian National Army (SNA) — a coalition of rebel groups — have brought Ankara into direct conflict with the SDF, even as both claim to be fighting ISIS.
The United States, with approximately 900 troops stationed in Syria, finds itself in a precarious position. It must balance its alliance with the SDF, crucial in countering ISIS, with its obligations to Turkey, a Nato ally. As local and international actors pursue their conflicting interests in Syria, the US risks being drawn deeper into a complex web of rivalries while attempting to prevent a resurgence of jihadist forces.
Russian general assassinated
In a high-profile act of targeted violence, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, a senior Russian military figure, was assassinated in Moscow this week. Kirillov, head of Russia’s Radiation, Chemical, and Biological Protection Forces, was killed along with his assistant Ilya Polikarpov when an explosive device concealed in an electric scooter detonated outside his apartment building.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
The assassination has been linked to Ukraine, with Russian authorities detaining a 29-year-old Uzbek man they claim was recruited by Ukrainian intelligence services. In a video released by the Russian Federal Security Services (FSB), the suspect, appearing handcuffed and visibly shaken, stated he had been offered $100,000 and a European passport to carry out the attack. The explosive device was reportedly delivered to him in Moscow, and he used a car equipped with a live-streaming camera to coordinate with organisers based in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro.
While Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) has not officially claimed responsibility, Ukrainian officials have called Kirillov a “legitimate target,” accusing him of overseeing the use of chemical weapons during Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Just a day before the assassination, Ukraine charged Kirillov in absentia for alleged war crimes, including the deployment of banned chemical agents. Moscow has dismissed these allegations, maintaining that it destroyed its chemical weapons stockpiles in 2017 in compliance with international treaties.
Kirillov’s killing marks the most significant assassination of a Russian military figure on home soil since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. The attack has sent shockwaves through Moscow, with President Vladimir Putin expressing his condolences and Russian officials vowing to bring those responsible to justice. The Russian Foreign Ministry has announced plans to raise the matter at the United Nations Security Council, framing the incident as a terrorist act orchestrated by Kyiv.
Images from the blast site reveal the devastating impact of the attack. The entrance to Kirillov’s apartment building in southeastern Moscow was badly damaged, with scorch marks on the walls and shattered windows. Two body bags were seen near the site, underscoring the deadly precision of the strike.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Kirillov’s death comes at a time of heightened tension and escalating violence in the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine. While Ukraine has not directly confirmed involvement, the assassination highlights a new phase in the war, where high-profile figures on both sides are increasingly targeted.
Kirillov’s role in the alleged use of chemical weapons made him a controversial figure internationally. The UK had previously sanctioned him over accusations of war crimes, and Ukraine’s SBU claims that under his leadership, Russia used chemical agents over 4,800 times during the war. Moscow denies these charges, framing Kirillov as a patriot and victim of Ukrainian aggression.
The attack also underscores the growing sophistication and reach of Ukrainian intelligence operations. If confirmed, it represents a significant escalation in the shadow war between the two nations, signalling Kyiv’s willingness to take the fight directly to Russia’s leadership. As the Kremlin scrambles to respond, the assassination could further escalate the conflict, both on the battlefield and beyond.

headline: Putin says Russia is ready to compromise with Trump on Ukraine war
description: Putin dismissed the idea of agreeing a temporary truce with Kyiv, saying only a long-lasting peace deal with Ukraine would suffice.
content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday that he was ready to compromise over Ukraine in possible talks with US President-elect Donald Trump on ending the war and had no conditions for starting talks with the Ukrainian authorities.
Trump, a self-styled master of brokering agreements and author of the 1987 book “Trump: the Art of the Deal”, has vowed to swiftly end the conflict, but has not yet given any details on how he might achieve that.
Putin, fielding questions on state TV during his annual question and answer session with Russians, told a reporter for a U.S. news channel that he was ready to meet Trump, whom he said he had not spoken to for years.
Also read | Russian President Putin opens his annual news conference, an event he uses to reinforce his authority
Asked what he might be able to offer Trump, Putin dismissed an assertion that Russia was in a weak position, saying that Russia had got much stronger since he ordered troops into Ukraine in 2022.

Watch | Before spat with Trump, Zelenskyy was asked why he is not wearing a suit. His reply
“We have always said that we are ready for negotiations and compromises,” Putin said, after saying that Russian forces, advancing across the entire front, were moving towards achieving their primary goals in Ukraine.
“Soon, those Ukrainians who want to fight will run out, in my opinion, soon there will be no one left who wants to fight. We are ready, but the other side needs to be ready for both negotiations and compromises.”
Reuters reported last month that Putin was open to discussing a Ukraine ceasefire deal with Trump, but ruled out making any major territorial concessions and insisted Kyiv abandon its ambitions to join NATO.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Putin said on Thursday that Russia had no conditions to start talks with Ukraine and was ready to negotiate with anyone, including President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
But he said any deal could only be signed with Ukraine’s legitimate authorities, which for now the Kremlin considered to be only the Ukrainian parliament.
Also read | Putin says he will ask Assad about the fate of American journalist who disappeared in Syria
Zelenskyy, whose term was due to expire earlier this year but has been extended due to martial law, would need to be re-elected for Moscow to consider him a legitimate signatory to any deal to ensure it was legally watertight, said Putin.
Putin dismissed the idea of agreeing a temporary truce with Kyiv, saying only a long-lasting peace deal with Ukraine would suffice.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Any talks should take as their starting point a preliminary agreement reached between Russian and Ukrainian negotiators in the early weeks of the war at talks in Istanbul, which was never implemented, he added.
Some Ukrainian politicians regard that draft deal as akin to a capitulation which would have neutered Ukraine’s military and political ambitions.
WAR
Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine has left tens of thousands of dead, displaced millions and triggered the biggest crisis in relations between Moscow and the West since the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis.
Russia, which casts the conflict as a defensive special military operation designed to stop dangerous NATO expansion to the east, controls around a fifth of Ukraine and has taken several thousand square kilometres of territory this year.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Determined to incorporate four Ukrainian regions into Russia, Moscow’s forces have taken village after village in the east and are now threatening strategically important cities such as Pokrovsk, a major road and rail hub.
Putin said the fighting was complex, so it was “difficult and pointless to guess what lies ahead… (but) we are moving, as you said, towards solving our primary tasks, which we outlined at the beginning of the special military operation.”
Also read | Putin lauds Modi’s ‘India First’ policy, says Russia will invest in India
Discussing the continued presence of Ukrainian forces in Russia’s Kursk region, Putin said Kyiv’s troops would be forced out, but declined to say exactly when that would happen.
The war has transformed the Russian economy and Putin said it was showing signs of overheating which was stoking worryingly high inflation. But he said growth was higher than many other economies such as Britain.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Asked if he’d do anything differently, he said he should have sent troops into Ukraine sooner than 2022 and that Russia should have been better prepared for the conflict.
Asked by a BBC reporter if he’d looked after Russia, something that Boris Yeltsin had asked him to do before handing over the presidency at the end of 1999, Putin said he had.”We have moved back from the edge of the abyss,” Putin said.
“I have done everything to ensure that Russia is an independent and sovereign power that is able to make decisions in its own interests.”
Russia, Putin said, had made proposals to Syria’s new rulers about Russia’s military bases there and most people that Moscow had spoken to on the issue favoured them staying.
Russia would need to think about whether the bases should remain or not, he added, but rumours about the death of Russian influence in the Middle East were exaggerated.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Putin touted what he said was the invincibility of the “Oreshnik” hypersonic missile that Russia has already test-fired at a Ukrainian military factory, saying he was ready to organise another launch at Ukraine and see if Western air defence systems could shoot it down.
In Brussels, Zelenskyy addressed Putin’s missile suggestion during a press conference at a European Council meeting, remarking of Putin: “Do you think he is a sane person?”

headline: At least 12 found dead at Indian restaurant in Georgia, authorities investigate

headline: ‘Wished to keep fighting’: Syria’s Assad in first comment after ouster
description: Assad said that “at no time during the events that have taken place in Syria” had he considered leaving the country
content:
On Monday, ousted Syrian President Bashar al-Assad—reportedly making his first remarks since the fall of Damascus a week ago—declared that he never intended to flee the country. However, he was evacuated by the Russian military after their base in western Syria came under attack.
Assad’s statement, shared on his Facebook page, detailed his evacuation by Russian military forces following an attack on their base in western Syria. He recounted leaving the capital on December 8, mere hours after insurgents breached its defenses. This departure, he insisted, was not an act of surrender but a strategic maneuver coordinated with his Russian allies, leading him to a secure location in the coastal province of Latakia.
However, the situation escalated when the Russian base itself came under drone attack, prompting a further evacuation to Russia later that same night. “I did not leave the country as part of a plan, as was reported earlier,” Assad said, adding, “At no point during these events did I consider stepping down or seeking refuge, nor was such a proposal made by any individual or party. The only course of action was to continue fighting against the terrorist onslaught.”
How Assad was pushed out 
After nearly 15 years of civil war, the final push to overthrow Assad took place in less than two weeks. On December 8, rebel forces seized control of the capital, Damascus, while Assad reportedly fled to an undisclosed location. Syria has been embroiled in civil war since 2011, following the Arab Spring, which saw widespread protests against authoritarian regimes. Hafez al-Assad ruled Syria with an iron fist from 1971 until his death in 2000, after which his son Bashar took over. Assad’s regime, dominated by the Alawite sect, faced discontent from the Sunni majority, especially amid rising unemployment and economic disparity. Initial peaceful protests were met with violent repression, escalating into armed conflict.
The conflict features a multitude of factions with varying goals and external support. The group that captured Damascus, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), emerged from al-Qaeda’s Syrian branch and seeks to establish a Sunni Islamic state. In contrast, the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), primarily Kurdish militias, aim for greater autonomy but are not direct enemies of Assad. The Turkey-backed Syrian National Army opposes both Assad and Kurdish forces. Foreign involvement complicates the situation further. Iran, Russia, and Hezbollah support Assad, while the US and Turkey back anti-Assad factions, primarily targeting the Kurds.
The recent fall of Damascus was attributed to diminished support for Assad from Iran and Russia, preoccupied with other conflicts. As the rebels advanced, they faced little resistance from the Syrian Army. Despite Assad’s unpopularity, many viewed him as a stabilizing force against Sunni extremism. His rise to power was unexpected; he was an ophthalmologist in London before becoming president. Initially perceived as a potential reformer, his brutal response to protests dashed hopes for liberalisation.

headline: Iranian singer arrested for performing online concert without hijab
description: Parastoo Ahmady was detained in Sari on Saturday, two days after posting her performance video on YouTube.
content:
Iranian authorities arrested 27-year-old singer Parastoo Ahmady Saturday after she performed an online concert on YouTube without wearing a hijab.
The video which went up on YouTube on Wednesday features Ahmady alongside four male musicians. In her post, she declared: “I am Parastoo, a girl who wants to sing for the people I love. This is a right I could not ignore; singing for the land I love passionately.” It has garnered over 1.4 million views.
The judiciary filed a case on the singer on Thursday, a day after her performance online.
On Saturday, Ahmady was detained in Sari, the capital of Mazandaran Province, according to Iranian lawyer Milad Panahipour. “Unfortunately, we do not know the charges against Ms Ahmady, who arrested her, or her place of detention, but we will follow up on the matter through legal authorities,” the lawyer was quoted as saying by news agency Associated Press (AP).

Panahipour also confirmed that two members of Ahmady’s band — Soheil Faghih Nasiri and Ehsan Beiraghdar –were arrested at their music studio in Tehran on the same day.
He also expressed concerns about the increasing crackdown on women’s freedoms in Iran, highlighting Ahmady’s case as an example of escalating tensions between authorities and those defying restrictions.

Since the Islamic Revolution of 1979, Iranian laws have prohibited women from singing solo before mixed-gender audiences or appearing without a hijab in the presence of unrelated men. Women can only perform in all-female audiences or as part of a chorus. The hijab has become both a religious requirement and a political symbol, mandatory since the years following the revolution.

Protests erupted across Iran in 2022 following the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini after she was detained by the morality police for allegedly not wearing her hijab properly. Though enforcement of the dress code softened briefly, authorities have recently adopted a stricter tone.

headline: Former prosecutor to represent suspect in UnitedHealthcare CEO’s killing
description: This development comes as Manhattan authorities work to extradite Mangione from Pennsylvania, where he was arrested earlier this week.
content:
Luigi Mangione, the 26-year-old suspect in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, has added Karen Friedman Agnifilo, a prominent former Manhattan prosecutor, to his legal team. This development comes as Manhattan authorities work to extradite Mangione from Pennsylvania, where he was arrested earlier this week.
Mangione was detained on Monday at a McDonald’s in Altoona, Pennsylvania, after a customer recognized him from mugshots released by law enforcement.
Police recovered a ghost gun, a mask, and a manifesto from Mangione at the time of his arrest. The handwritten manifesto reportedly condemned corporations for exploiting the American public, with specific criticism aimed at healthcare companies like UnitedHealthcare.
Karen Friedman Agnifilo, Mangione’s new attorney, has an extensive legal background, having served as the Chief Assistant District Attorney in Manhattan. Her law firm, Agnifilo Intrater LLP, confirmed her involvement but stated she would not comment on the case at this time.

Mangione is currently held without bail in Pennsylvania, facing charges of murder, weapons possession, and forgery in New York. While his Pennsylvania lawyer has indicated Mangione may contest extradition, Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg has stated that steps are in place to ensure his transfer.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul is also prepared to request intervention from Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro if necessary.
Brian Thompson, a leading figure in the healthcare industry, was shot outside the New York Hilton Midtown on December 4 while heading to an investor conference. Witnesses said the suspected attacker fired multiple rounds at Thompson from a distance of 20 feet before fleeing the scene.

headline: Hezbollah chief says group lost its supply route through Syria
description: "Yes, Hezbollah has lost the military supply route through Syria at this stage, but this loss is a detail in the resistance's work," Qassem said in a televised speech on Saturday, without mentioning Assad by name.
content:
Hezbollah head Naim Qassem said on Saturday that the Lebanese armed group had lost its supply route through Syria, in his first comments since the toppling of President Bashar al-Assad nearly a week ago by a sweeping rebel offensive.
Under Assad, Iran-backed Hezbollah used Syria to bring in weapons and other military equipment from Iran, through Iraq and Syria and into Lebanon. But on Dec. 6, anti-Assad fighters seized the border with Iraq and cut off that route, and two days later, Islamist rebels captured the capital Damascus.
“Yes, Hezbollah has lost the military supply route through Syria at this stage, but this loss is a detail in the resistance’s work,” Qassem said in a televised speech on Saturday, without mentioning Assad by name.
“A new regime could come and this route could return to normal, and we could look for other ways,” he added.
Hezbollah started intervening in Syria in 2013 to help Assad fight rebels seeking to topple him at that time. Last week, as rebels approached Damascus, the group sent supervising officers to oversee a withdrawal of its fighters there.
More than 50 years of Assad family rule has now been replaced with a transitional caretaker government put in place by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, a former al Qaeda affiliate that spearheaded the rebel offensive.
Qassem said Hezbollah “cannot judge these new forces until they stabilise” and “take clear positions”, but said he hoped that the Lebanese and Syrian peoples and governments could continue to cooperate.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“We also hope that this new ruling party will consider Israel an enemy and not normalise relations with it. These are the headlines that will affect the nature of the relationship between us and Syria,” Qassem said.
Hezbollah and Israel exchanged fire across Lebanon’s southern border for nearly a year in hostilities triggered by the Gaza war, before Israel went on the offensive in September, killing most of Hezbollah’s top leadership.

headline: Indian-American OpenAI whistleblower Suchir Balaji found dead in US apartment
description: Balaji’s death has reignited debates about the ethical and legal implications of AI technologies.
content:
Suchir Balaji, an Indian-American former researcher at OpenAI who had publicly criticised the company’s practices, was found dead in his San Francisco apartment on November 26.
The 26-year-old’s death has been ruled a suicide, with authorities reporting no evidence of foul play.
Balaji, who left OpenAI in August after four years, was a prominent voice raising ethical concerns about the use of copyrighted materials to train generative AI models like ChatGPT.
“I recently participated in a New York Times story about fair use and generative AI, and why I’m sceptical ‘fair use’ would be a plausible defence for a lot of generative AI products. I also wrote a blog post about the nitty-gritty details of fair use and why I believe this,” Balaji had written on X.
I recently participated in a NYT story about fair use and generative AI, and why I’m skeptical “fair use” would be a plausible defense for a lot of generative AI products. I also wrote a blog post (https://t.co/xhiVyCk2Vk) about the nitty-gritty details of fair use and why I…
— Suchir Balaji (@suchirbalaji) October 23, 2024
In a separate interview with the New York Times, Balaji described OpenAI’s approach to data collection as harmful. “If you believe what I believe, you have to just leave the company,” he said, expressing concern over the training of GPT-4 on massive amounts of internet data.

Balaji’s concerns centred on how generative AI systems could produce outputs that compete with the original copyrighted works used in their training. In a blog post cited by the Chicago Tribune, he argued, “No known factors seem to weigh in favour of ChatGPT being a fair use of its training data.” He noted that this issue extended beyond OpenAI, saying, “Fair use and generative AI is a much broader issue than any one product or company.”
